summary: Describes UDP-Lite, a variant of UDP that lets an application say how much of each packet the checksum must cover. Packets with damage outside that area can still be delivered, which suits audio and video that tolerate some bit errors, especially on noisy links. With full coverage it behaves like UDP.

plainLanguage.summary: UDP-Lite lets an application protect only the part of a packet that must arrive unchanged. A receiver can still deliver a packet with damage beyond that protected part, but the application must decide whether the remaining data is useful.

questions: how does udp-lite checksum coverage work
subtitle: A UDP-style transport that lets an application choose how much of each packet the checksum protects.

tldr.problem: Some voice and video applications can tolerate errors in part of a payload, but ordinary UDP checksum handling protects the whole packet or no payload at all.
tldr.mechanism: UDP-Lite replaces UDP's Length field with Checksum Coverage. The checksum always protects the UDP-Lite header and may leave the rest of the payload unchecked, as chosen by the sending application.
tldr.outcome: With full-packet coverage, UDP-Lite is semantically identical to UDP. It uses IP protocol number 136 and RFC 3828 is updated by RFC 6335.

today: RFC 3828 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 6335. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Allow Partly Damaged Packets
sections.content:
Some voice and video codecs can cope better with a few damaged payload bits than with losing an entire packet. On an error-prone link, a link layer may be able to forward a packet when errors occur only in data the application considers less sensitive.

UDP-Lite provides an optional partial checksum coverage for this case. The sender identifies a protected part and an unprotected part. Damage in the unprotected part does not make the transport layer discard the packet. Full coverage remains the recommended default, in which case UDP-Lite behaves like UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: Some applications can use a packet even when part of its payload has errors. UDP-Lite can deliver such a packet if the errors are outside the part covered by its checksum.

sections.title: The UDP-Lite Header and Coverage Field
sections.content:
The UDP-Lite header keeps the UDP Source Port and Destination Port fields, then has Checksum Coverage and Checksum. Each field is 16 bits. The Length field used by UDP is replaced because the IP layer provides the packet length.

Checksum Coverage counts octets from the first octet of the UDP-Lite header. The header is always covered. A value of zero means the checksum covers the entire packet; any other valid value is at least 8. A receiver MUST discard a packet with coverage from 1 through 7 or coverage greater than the IP length. An application asking for no payload protection uses coverage 8.
sections.plainLanguage: The header names the ports and tells the receiver how many starting octets the checksum protects. The header itself is always protected; zero means the whole packet is covered.

sections.title: Checksum Calculation
sections.content:
The checksum is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's-complement sum of an IP-derived pseudo-header and the covered UDP-Lite octets. If an odd number of octets is covered, a zero octet is added for the calculation. The checksum field is zero while the calculation is made; a calculated zero is transmitted as all ones.

The pseudo-header includes the IP addresses and protocol information. Its length comes from the IP module, not from a UDP-Lite Length field, and counts the UDP-Lite header plus the rest of the IP payload. This allows the receiving IP module to supply the complete packet length.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender calculates a checksum over the protected bytes and information from the IP header. The receiver repeats that calculation to detect errors in the protected part.

sections.title: Application, IP and Link Responsibilities
sections.content:
An application interface should let a sender choose Checksum Coverage and let a receiver learn the coverage or reject packets below its own threshold. The default SHOULD cover the entire packet. Applications that accept partly unchecked data must not assume that data is correct and should perform any validity checks they need.

The IP module supplies the pseudo-header and MUST NOT add padding to the IP payload. For a jumbogram, zero covers the full packet; otherwise the 16-bit coverage field can cover at most the first 65535 octets. A link that supports partial error detection may use the coverage value as a hint, but it must still detect errors in the sensitive portion. A link without that ability must check the whole packet.

UDP-Lite only changes delivery when the link layer also supports partial error detection. Without that support, damaged packets are handled as they are for UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: The application chooses the coverage and must treat bytes beyond it as possibly damaged. A link only gains the option to pass those bytes through if it can protect the covered part separately.

sections.title: Compatibility with UDP
sections.content:
UDP-Lite uses UDP's port number assignments and similar syntax. Applications designed for UDP may use UDP-Lite with full packet coverage, and the RFC says only minor changes to a UDP implementation are needed.

UDP-Lite has its own IP protocol identifier, 136, so a receiver can distinguish it from UDP. A host that does not recognize UDP-Lite will generally return an ICMP Protocol Unreachable or ICMPv6 Payload Type Unknown error. The separate identifier avoids a partially covered UDP-Lite packet being silently discarded by a UDP receiver after a checksum mismatch.
sections.plainLanguage: UDP-Lite has a distinct IP identifier, so a host can tell it apart from UDP. Full coverage gives applications UDP-like behavior.

sections.title: Security and Integrity
sections.content:
Partial coverage allows the unprotected part of a packet to change in transit. Authentication that checks the whole packet will therefore fail if that part is damaged. IPsec integrity checks cover at least the whole IP payload, so they discard corruption in any protected bit and remove UDP-Lite's partial-coverage benefit.

Encryption can also make damaged data unusable because many encryption methods spread errors. The RFC warns that omitting integrity checks can in some circumstances weaken confidentiality, and that an attacker may cause predictable changes to plaintext when a stream cipher is used without an integrity check.
sections.plainLanguage: Partial coverage permits some bytes to change, which conflicts with security checks that require the whole packet to remain unchanged. Applications must consider how authentication and encryption interact with that choice.

fields.name: Source Port
fields.desc: Port number of the sending process.

fields.name: Destination Port
fields.desc: Port number of the receiving process.

fields.name: Checksum Coverage
fields.desc: Protected octets from the start of the header; zero covers the whole packet.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: Checks the pseudo-header and covered octets.
